extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of social science, political economy, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how to apply the inverse-deductive (historical) and direct-deductive methods in social science, including criteria for carving separate branches (e.g., political economy), verification by experience, and the role of national character (political ethology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive conclusions are hypothetical and contingent on supposed circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive science conclusions "are therefore, in the strictest sense of the word, hypothetical. They are grounded on some suppositious set of circumstances, and declare how some given cause would operate in those circumstances, supposing that no others were combined with them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use deductive reasoning only as a conditional statement: conclusions hold only to the extent the supposed circumstances match the real case. To approach concrete truth, increase the number of individualizing circumstances in the premises; otherwise treat results as hypothetical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit applicability of the deductive method to phenomena mainly governed by few causes
rubrics_metrics.description: "This mode of inquiry... must, therefore, on pain of frivolity, be limited to those classes of social facts which... are under the immediate influence, principally at least, of a few only."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying simple deductive models to social facts heavily influenced by many interacting causes. Prefer deduction where a small number of causes predominate; otherwise results accumulate uncertainty rapidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification for distinct branches: different immediate causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Different species of social facts are "in the main dependent, immediately and in the first resort, on different kinds of causes; and therefore not only may with advantage, but must, be studied apart."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create separate departmental sciences when the immediately determining causes differ across phenomena (e.g., study industrial phenomena separately from moral or political phenomena), while recognizing interdependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for carving a departmental science
rubrics_metrics.description: A department may be formed when phenomena "do mainly depend, at least in the first resort, on one class of circumstances only; and that even when other circumstances interfere, the ascertainment of the effect due to the one class of circumstances alone, is a sufficiently intricate and difficult business to make it expedient to perform it once for all."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form a specialized discipline when (a) a dominant class of causes primarily determines a set of phenomena and (b) isolating and analyzing that class is itself a complex but worthwhile task that can later be corrected for other influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political Economy as methodological example: treat one motive as sole for analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Political economy "makes entire abstraction of every other human passion or motive; except those which may be regarded as perpetually antagonizing principles to the desire of wealth... Political Economy considers mankind as occupied solely in acquiring and consuming wealth; and aims at showing what is the course of action into which mankind... would be impelled, if that motive... were absolute ruler of all their actions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idealizing assumptions (e.g., preference for more wealth) to isolate a dominant motive; treat this as a tractable hypothesis to be corrected later by accounting for counter-motives (e.g., aversion to labor, desire for present enjoyment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Check applicability of disciplinary conclusions against differing social premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Conclusions adapted to a society thus constituted "require to be revised whenever they are applied to any other."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying theory across contexts, trace premises back and replace them with the appropriate premises for the new context (e.g., different property relations, degree of competition). Beware of assuming immutability of social arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by Specific Experience is indispensable
rubrics_metrics.description: The indispensable element in deductive sciences is "Verification by Specific Experience—comparison between the conclusions of reasoning and the results of observation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect empirical facts or statistics to collate with theoretical deductions. Verification is required to test whether the theory's conditional conclusions hold in observed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare observed facts into empirical laws for collating with theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A preparatory treatment of observed facts consists in "finding general propositions which express concisely what is common to large classes of observed facts; and these are called the empirical laws of the phenomena."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistics and historical generalizations to summarize observations into empirical laws that theory can be checked against. This preparation is often necessary to enable collocation with deductive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical generalizations only transferable when remote causes are stable
rubrics_metrics.description: An empirical law "can only be relied on as applicable to unobserved cases, so long as there is reason to think that no change has taken place in any of the remote causes on which the immediate causes depend."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before applying a statistical generalization to new cases, investigate remoter causes to ensure they have not changed; otherwise empirical laws may mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deductive theory must supervise empirical inference (theory as sentinel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even where conclusions from specific observation are available, "it is necessary that the deductive science should stand sentinel over the whole process; that it should be constantly referred to, and its sanction obtained to every inference."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theory to interpret empirical findings, to avoid misapplying statistical regularities. Theory guides which variables to consider and which differences of circumstance invalidate empirical transfers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct verification often impossible for single causes among many
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the effect of any one social cause among many, "the effect is... so much disguised by the similar or contrary effects of other influencing agents, that specific experience can at most only show that on the average... the cases where there were [the cause] exhibited the effect in a greater degree than those where there were not."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limits of single-case experiments in social contexts; exact replication of theoretical circumstances is generally infeasible, so direct experimental verification is often unavailable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect verification through multiple instances and explanatory scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The individual case is "verified indirectly, by the verification of other conclusions, drawn in other individual cases from the same laws."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strengthen a theory by showing it explains and predicts a range of independent cases; success across varied instances increases trust even when direct verification of the original instance is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competence-to-predict test: theory must explain present and past
rubrics_metrics.description: "To prove... that our science... render[s] us competent to predict the future, we must show that they would have enabled us to predict the present and the past."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A usable social theory should be able to account for existing general facts and historical phenomena; inability to do so signals incompleteness or error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle unexplained residual phenomena by searching circumstances or improving theory
rubrics_metrics.description: If something was not predicted, "this constitutes a residual phenomenon, requiring further study... we must either search among the circumstances of the particular case until we find one... or we must... seek the explanation by an extension and improvement of the theory itself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat anomalies as diagnostic: either identify omitted local causes or expand/refine theoretical assumptions. Do not ignore residuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define 'state of society' as simultaneous condition of many interrelated features
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'state of society' is "the simultaneous state of all the greater social facts or phenomena" (knowledge, industry, wealth distribution, classes, beliefs, tastes, government, laws, customs, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theorizing about societal conditions, consider the whole constellation of interdependent social facts rather than isolated variables; look for regular co-existence patterns among these features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search for uniformities of co-existence and laws of succession
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist "Uniformities of Co-existence between the states of the various social phenomena" and the fundamental problem is "to find the laws according to which any state of society produces the state which succeeds it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical/social inquiry should aim to discover systematic correlations (co-existence) and causal rules (succession) among societal features across time and places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for progressiveness/change across generations in historical method
rubrics_metrics.description: Social sciences are conversant with subject-matter "whose properties are changeable... from age to age" owing to reciprocal action of effects upon causes; periods of one generation mark distinct changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical methods must account for cumulative, generational change (progress or trajectory) in character and institutions; do not assume static human nature across epochs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not isolate fields heavily entangled with national character (no separate Science of Government)
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be "no separate Science of Government; that being the fact which, of all others, is most mixed up, both as cause and effect, with the qualities of the particular people or of the particular age."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating government in isolation when it is deeply interwoven with national character and other social conditions; such topics belong to the general science of society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate Political Ethology: laws of national character are central and understudied
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of national (or collective) character "are by far the most important class of sociological laws... the causes of national character are scarcely at all understood... the character... enters largely into the production of all the other phenomena."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigation of how institutions and circumstances shape collective character is crucial for applying other branches (e.g., political economy) in practice; neglecting ethology undermines applied validity.
